claim: The ILK/PINCH/Parvin (IPP) complex interacts with actin filaments to regulate the cytoskeleton-FA crosstalk.
source: As a core platform to organize FA proteins, the tripartite ILK/PINCH/Parvin (IPP) complex interacts with actin filaments to regulate the cytoskeleton-FA crosstalk.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established knowledge in the field and citations to prior work.

claim: Rsu1 is enriched in FA through PINCH1.
source: Rsu1, a Ras suppressor, is enriched in FA through PINCH1 and plays important roles in regulating F-actin structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research and established knowledge.

claim: Rsu1 plays important roles in regulating F-actin structures.
source: Rsu1, a Ras suppressor, is enriched in FA through PINCH1 and plays important roles in regulating F-actin structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research and established knowledge.

claim: The leucine-rich-repeats of Rsu1 form a solenoid structure.
source: Here, we solved crystal structures of the Rsu1/PINCH1 complex, in which the leucine-rich-repeats of Rsu1 form a solenoid structure to tightly associate with the C-terminal region of PINCH1.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The leucine-rich-repeats of Rsu1 tightly associate with the C-terminal region of PINCH1.
source: Here, we solved crystal structures of the Rsu1/PINCH1 complex, in which the leucine-rich-repeats of Rsu1 form a solenoid structure to tightly associate with the C-terminal region of PINCH1.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The interaction between Rsu1 and PINCH1 blocks the IPP-mediated F-actin bundling by disrupting the binding of PINCH1 to actin.
source: Further structural analysis uncovered that the interaction between Rsu1 and PINCH1 blocks the IPP-mediated F-actin bundling by disrupting the binding of PINCH1 to actin.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis and inference from the data.

claim: Overexpressing Rsu1 in HeLa cells impairs stress fiber formation.
source: Consistently, overexpressing Rsu1 in HeLa cells impairs stress fiber formation and cell spreading.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell-based assays.

claim: Overexpressing Rsu1 in HeLa cells impairs cell spreading.
source: Consistently, overexpressing Rsu1 in HeLa cells impairs stress fiber formation and cell spreading.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell-based assays.

claim: Rsu1 is critical for tuning the communication between F-actin and FA by interacting with the IPP complex.
source: Together, our findings demonstrated that Rsu1 is critical for tuning the communication between F-actin and FA by interacting with the IPP complex and negatively modulating the F-actin bundling.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined structural and cellular data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rsu1 negatively modulates F-actin bundling.
source: Together, our findings demonstrated that Rsu1 is critical for tuning the communication between F-actin and FA by interacting with the IPP complex and negatively modulating the F-actin bundling.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined structural and cellular data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Integrin-mediated focal adhesions link the extracellular matrix to intracellular integrin adhesion complex and regulate F-actin dynamics.
source: Integrin-mediated focal adhesions (FAs) link the extracellular matrix (ECM) to intracellular integrin adhesion complex (IAC) and regulate F-actin dynamics (Calderwood et al., 2000; Geiger et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The IPP complex acts as an essential platform to recruit many proteins for FA formation and signaling.
source: Among the IAC components, tripartite integrin-linked kinase (ILK) associates with another two key players PINCH and Parvin to form the ILK/PINCH/Parvin (IPP) complex, which acts as an essential platform to recruit many proteins for the FA formation and signaling and provide a linkage between FA and actin cytoskeleton (Legate et al., 2006; Qin and Wu, 2012; Tu et al., 2001; Wickström et al., 2010; Wu, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The IPP complex provides a linkage between FA and actin cytoskeleton.
source: Among the IAC components, tripartite integrin-linked kinase (ILK) associates with another two key players PINCH and Parvin to form the ILK/PINCH/Parvin (IPP) complex, which acts as an essential platform to recruit many proteins for the FA formation and signaling and provide a linkage between FA and actin cytoskeleton (Legate et al., 2006; Qin and Wu, 2012; Tu et al., 2001; Wickström et al., 2010; Wu, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ILK is a pseudokinase.
source: As a pseudokinase, ILK connects PINCH and Parvin through its N-terminal ankyrin repeat domain and C-terminal kinase domain, respectively (Chiswell et al., 2008; Fukuda et al., 2009; Tu et al., 2001; Velyvis et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ILK connects PINCH and Parvin through its N-terminal ankyrin repeat domain and C-terminal kinase domain, respectively.
source: As a pseudokinase, ILK connects PINCH and Parvin through its N-terminal ankyrin repeat domain and C-terminal kinase domain, respectively (Chiswell et al., 2008; Fukuda et al., 2009; Tu et al., 2001; Velyvis et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Dysfunctions of the three IPP proteins result in a number of diseases including different types of cancers, diabetes, and heart failure.
source: Dysfunctions of the three IPP proteins result in a number of diseases including different types of cancers, diabetes, and heart failure (Cabodi et al., 2010; Hannigan et al., 2005; Qin and Wu, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rsu1 is a leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-containing protein conserved from human to worms.
source: Ras suppressor protein 1 (Rsu1), a leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-containing protein conserved from human to worms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), was recognized as a major FA component (Horton et al., 2015) and is important for FA formation and cell motility (Simpson et al., 2008; Winograd-Katz et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a reference to a figure showing sequence conservation and citations to prior research.

claim: Rsu1 was recognized as a major FA component.
source: Ras suppressor protein 1 (Rsu1), a leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-containing protein conserved from human to worms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), was recognized as a major FA component (Horton et al., 2015) and is important for FA formation and cell motility (Simpson et al., 2008; Winograd-Katz et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Rsu1 is important for FA formation and cell motility.
source: Ras suppressor protein 1 (Rsu1), a leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-containing protein conserved from human to worms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), was recognized as a major FA component (Horton et al., 2015) and is important for FA formation and cell motility (Simpson et al., 2008; Winograd-Katz et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rsu1 was first identified to suppress Ras-dependent oncogenic transformation.
source: Rsu1 was first identified to suppress Ras-dependent oncogenic transformation, during which the cells show typical anchorage-independent growth and morphological change (Cutler et al., 1992; Masuelli and Cutler, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rsu1 expression level is upregulated in certain types of cancer cells.
source: However, Rsu1 appears to possess multiple functions in cancer, as its expression level is upregulated in certain types of cancer cells and abnormally high expression level of Rsu1 may also contribute to cancer metastasis (Gkretsi et al., 2017; Louca et al., 2020; Zacharia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Abnormally high expression level of Rsu1 may contribute to cancer metastasis.
source: However, Rsu1 appears to possess multiple functions in cancer, as its expression level is upregulated in certain types of cancer cells and abnormally high expression level of Rsu1 may also contribute to cancer metastasis (Gkretsi et al., 2017; Louca et al., 2020; Zacharia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vertebrates express two PINCH proteins, PINCH1 and PINCH2, each consisting of a tandem array of five LIM domains.
source: Vertebrates express two PINCH proteins, PINCH1 and PINCH2, each consisting of a tandem array of five LIM domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by a reference to a figure and established knowledge.

claim: Rsu1 was reported to interact with the C-terminal LIM (LIM5) domain of PINCH1.
source: Rsu1 was reported to interact with the C-terminal LIM (LIM5) domain of PINCH1 (Dougherty et al., 2005; Kadrmas et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rsu1 and PINCH1 concert to control cell adhesion, migration and apoptosis by integrating Ras and integrin signaling.
source: By integrating Ras and integrin signaling, Rsu1 and PINCH1 concert to control cell adhesion, migration and apoptosis (Dougherty et al., 2005; Dougherty et al., 2008; Kadrmas et al., 2004; Montanez et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Depletion of Rsu1 in cultured cells and Drosophila led to the reduced expression of PINCH1 and ILK.
source: Depletion of Rsu1 in cultured cells and Drosophila led to the reduced expression of PINCH1 and ILK, thus impairing the FA formation and the F-actin organization (Dougherty et al., 2005; Gonzalez-Nieves et al., 2013; Kadrmas et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Depletion of Rsu1 impairs FA formation and F-actin organization.
source: Depletion of Rsu1 in cultured cells and Drosophila led to the reduced expression of PINCH1 and ILK, thus impairing the FA formation and the F-actin organization (Dougherty et al., 2005; Gonzalez-Nieves et al., 2013; Kadrmas et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Overexpressing Rsu1 damaged stress fibers.
source: However, although Rsu1 was suggested to maintain the cellular protein level of the IPP complex that is important for the F-actin organization at the FA (Legate et al., 2006; Wickström et al., 2010), overexpressing Rsu1 damaged stress fibers, the cross-linked F-actin bundles anchored at the FAs in cells (Masuelli and Cutler, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Rsu1 negatively regulates F-actin organization in muscle by inhibiting PINCH's activity in Drosophila.
source: In addition, a recent study in Drosophila indicated that Rsu1 negatively regulates F-actin organization in muscle by inhibiting PINCH's activity (Green et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The IPP complex promotes F-actin bundling by using two actin-binding motifs from PINCH and Parvin respectively.
source: Because the IPP complex was shown to promote F-actin bundling by using two actin-binding motifs from PINCH and Parvin respectively (Vaynberg et al., 2018), it is intriguing to unveil how Rsu1 coordinates its reversed effects in the destabilization of F-actin and the stabilization of the IPP complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The C-terminal region of PINCH1 containing either the LIM4 and LIM5 domains (LIM45C, aa.188–325) or the LIM5 domain (LIM5C, aa.249–325) shows strong binding affinity to Rsu1 with a dissociation constant of ~15 nM.
source: The C-terminal region of PINCH1 containing either the LIM4 and LIM5 domains (LIM45C, aa.188–325) or the LIM5 domain (LIM5C, aa.249–325) shows the strong binding affinity to Rsu1 with a dissociation constant of ~15 nM (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The very C-terminal sequence (aa.308–325) in PINCH1 is indispensable for the binding of PINCH1 to Rsu1.
source: Interestingly, the very C-terminal sequence (aa.308–325) in PINCH1 is indispensable for the binding of PINCH1 to Rsu1, as the LIM5 domain alone without this C-terminal sequence lost the Rsu1-binding ability (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The removal of the C-terminal region (aa.216–277) of Rsu1 (Rsu1ΔC) affected little to the complex formation of Rsu1 and PINCH1.
source: On the other hand, the removal of the C-terminal region (aa.216–277) of Rsu1 (Rsu1ΔC) that does not belong to the LRR motif (Kobe and Deisenhofer, 1994) affected little to the complex formation of Rsu1 and PINCH1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the LRR-region is sufficient for the Rsu1/PINCH1 interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The LRR-region is sufficient for the Rsu1/PINCH1 interaction.
source: On the other hand, the removal of the C-terminal region (aa.216–277) of Rsu1 (Rsu1ΔC) that does not belong to the LRR motif (Kobe and Deisenhofer, 1994) affected little to the complex formation of Rsu1 and PINCH1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the LRR-region is sufficient for the Rsu1/PINCH1 interaction.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that removal of the C-terminal region does not affect binding.

claim: The complex structures of Rsu1ΔC/PINCH1_LIM5C with one crystal form at 1.65 Å resolution and Rsu1/PINCH1_LIM45C with two different crystal forms at 2.2 Å and 3.15 Å resolution respectively were determined by the molecular replacement method.
source: The complex structures of Rsu1ΔC/PINCH1_LIM5C with one crystal form at 1.65 Å resolution and Rsu1/PINCH1_LIM45C with two different crystal forms at 2.2 Å and 3.15 Å resolution respectively were determined by the molecular replacement method (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: The nine LRRs of Rsu1 form a curved solenoid capped by the helical regions in the both N- and C-termini.
source: In the Rsu1/PINCH1_LIM45C complex, the nine LRRs of Rsu1 form a curved solenoid capped by the helical regions in the both N- and C-termini, named N-cap and C-cap, respectively (Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The N-cap consists of the α1-helix.
source: The N-cap consists of the α1-helix while the C-cap contains three α-helices (α2–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: The C-cap contains three α-helices (α2–4).
source: The N-cap consists of the α1-helix while the C-cap contains three α-helices (α2–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: Both the N-cap and C-cap cap the LRR-solenoid by forming extensive hydrophobic interactions with LRR1–2 and LRR8–9, respectively.
source: Both the two helical regions cap the LRR-solenoid by forming extensive hydrophobic interactions with LRR1–2 and LRR8–9, respectively (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: All the nine LRRs adopt the typical LRR-folding by using conserved leucine residues to form the hydrophobic core except for a few short loops inserted in LRR1, 5, and 9.
source: All the nine LRRs adopt the typical LRR-folding by using conserved leucine residues to form the hydrophobic core except for a few short loops inserted in LRR1, 5, and 9 (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The deletion of C-cap results in the disruption of LRR9 in the Rsu1ΔC/PINCH1_LIM5C complex.
source: Consistently, the deletion of C-cap results in the disruption of LRR9 in the Rsu1ΔC/PINCH1_LIM5C complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The LRR-solenoid of Rsu1 interacts with both the LIM5 domain and the C-terminal tail of PINCH1 through the concave surface of the solenoid.
source: Consistent with our biochemical finding, the LRR-solenoid of Rsu1 interacts with both the LIM5 domain and the C-terminal tail (C-tail, folded as a α-helix) of PINCH1 through the concave surface of the solenoid, mainly formed by the parallel β-sheet and the flanking loop regions (Figure 2A,B,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The LIM5C fragment in PINCH1 and the LRRs in Rsu1 showed the essentially same conformation with the overall RMSD of ~0.3 Å in all three complex structures.
source: In all three complex structures that we solved, the LIM5C fragment in PINCH1 and the LRRs in Rsu1 showed the essentially same conformation with the overall RMSD of ~0.3 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The LIM4 domain in PINCH1 adopts different orientations as observed in the two crystal forms of the Rsu1/PINCH1_LIM45C complex.
source: However, the LIM4 domain in PINCH1 adopts different orientations as observed in the two crystal forms of the Rsu1/PINCH1_LIM45C complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating the intrinsic, structural flexibility between the LIM4 and LIM5 domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: There is intrinsic structural flexibility between the LIM4 and LIM5 domains.
source: However, the LIM4 domain in PINCH1 adopts different orientations as observed in the two crystal forms of the Rsu1/PINCH1_LIM45C complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), indicating the intrinsic, structural flexibility between the LIM4 and LIM5 domains.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of different orientations in different crystal forms.

claim: The Rsu1/PINCH1 interaction buries a large surface area of ~1100 Å2 for each protein.
source: In line with the nM-scale binding affinity, the Rsu1/PINCH1 interaction buries a large surface area of ~1100 Å2 for each protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of the complex.

claim: The PINCH1-binding surface on Rsu1 is conserved from human to worm.
source: The PINCH1-binding surface on Rsu1 is conserved from human to worm (Figure 3A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence conservation analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Both PINCH1 and PINCH2 interact with Rsu1 in different species using the same binding mode.
source: Given the highly conserved feature of the LIM45C region in all PINCH homologues (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), it is very likely that both PINCH1 and PINCH2 interacts with Rsu1 in different species using the same binding mode found in our structures.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the high conservation of the LIM45C region across PINCH homologues.

claim: PINCH2_LIM5C forms a stable complex with Rsu1 in solution.
source: However, although the analytical gel filtration analysis showed that PINCH2_LIM5C forms a stable complex with Rsu1 in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), the binding of PINCH2_LIM5C to Rsu1 showed an affinity 100-fold weaker than the binding of PINCH1_LIM5C to Rsu1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), presumably due to the substitution of a few interface residues, such as F253 and H254 in PINCH1 replaced by a tyrosine and an asparagine in PINCH2, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by gel filtration data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The binding of PINCH2_LIM5C to Rsu1 showed an affinity 100-fold weaker than the binding of PINCH1_LIM5C to Rsu1.
source: However, although the analytical gel filtration analysis showed that PINCH2_LIM5C forms a stable complex with Rsu1 in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), the binding of PINCH2_LIM5C to Rsu1 showed an affinity 100-fold weaker than the binding of PINCH1_LIM5C to Rsu1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), presumably due to the substitution of a few interface residues, such as F253 and H254 in PINCH1 replaced by a tyrosine and an asparagine in PINCH2, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The weaker binding of PINCH2 to Rsu1 is presumably due to the substitution of a few interface residues, such as F253 and H254 in PINCH1 replaced by a tyrosine and an asparagine in PINCH2, respectively.
source: However, although the analytical gel filtration analysis showed that PINCH2_LIM5C forms a stable complex with Rsu1 in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), the binding of PINCH2_LIM5C to Rsu1 showed an affinity 100-fold weaker than the binding of PINCH1_LIM5C to Rsu1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), presumably due to the substitution of a few interface residues, such as F253 and H254 in PINCH1 replaced by a tyrosine and an asparagine in PINCH2, respectively.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on structural and binding data.

claim: Upon binding to Rsu1, the C-terminal α-helix in PINCH1 undergoes a substantial conformational change as compared with the apo structure of PINCH1_LIM5C.
source: Upon binding to Rsu1, the C-terminal α-helix in PINCH1 undergoes a substantial conformational change as compared with the apo structure of PINCH1_LIM5C (Figure 3B; Vaynberg et al., 2018), while the conformation of the LIM5 domain remains largely unchanged.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in the referenced figure and citation.

claim: The conformation of the LIM5 domain remains largely unchanged upon binding to Rsu1.
source: Upon binding to Rsu1, the C-terminal α-helix in PINCH1 undergoes a substantial conformational change as compared with the apo structure of PINCH1_LIM5C (Figure 3B; Vaynberg et al., 2018), while the conformation of the LIM5 domain remains largely unchanged.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The large PINCH1-binding surface on Rsu1 extends from LRR2 to LRR9.
source: The large PINCH1-binding surface on Rsu1 extends from LRR2 to LRR9 (Figure 2F), in which 22 surface residues form hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, and hydrophobic interactions with PINCH1_LIM5C (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: 22 surface residues on Rsu1 form hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, and hydrophobic interactions with PINCH1_LIM5C.
source: The large PINCH1-binding surface on Rsu1 extends from LRR2 to LRR9 (Figure 2F), in which 22 surface residues form hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, and hydrophobic interactions with PINCH1_LIM5C (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Two buried water molecules conserved in both the Rsu1ΔC/PINCH1_LIM5C and Rsu1/PINCH1_LIM45C complex structures critically coordinate three clusters of the polar interactions.
source: In this network, two buried water molecules, conserved in both the Rsu1ΔC/PINCH1_LIM5C and Rsu1/PINCH1_LIM45C complex structures (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), critically coordinate three clusters of the polar interactions as highlighted in Figure 3D.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The Y140K mutation in Rsu1 decreased the binding affinity by ~100 fold.
source: In Rsu1, the Y140K mutation that disrupts the cation-π interaction between Y140Rsu1 and K297PINCH1, decreased the binding affinity by ~100 fold as indicated by ITC (Figure 3E), and the D115K/Y140K (DY/KK) double mutation further diminished the Rsu1/PINCH1 interaction (Figure 3E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3E) presumably due to the introduction of an additional charge repulsion in the binding interface.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The D115K/Y140K (DY/KK) double mutation further diminished the Rsu1/PINCH1 interaction.
source: In Rsu1, the Y140K mutation that disrupts the cation-π interaction between Y140Rsu1 and K297PINCH1, decreased the binding affinity by ~100 fold as indicated by ITC (Figure 3E), and the D115K/Y140K (DY/KK) double mutation further diminished the Rsu1/PINCH1 interaction (Figure 3E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3E) presumably due to the introduction of an additional charge repulsion in the binding interface.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The charge-reversing mutations (K297D and D295K) in PINCH1 either dramatically weakened or abolished the binding of PINCH1 to Rsu1.
source: Likewise, the charge-reversing mutations (K297D and D295K) in PINCH1 either dramatically weakened or abolished the binding of PINCH1 to Rsu1 (Figure 3E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The C-terminal α-helix of PINCH1 has been shown to directly interact with actin.
source: Previously, the C-terminal α-helix of PINCH1 has been shown to directly interact with actin and is required for the IPP-mediated bundling of F-actin, a process important for cell spreading and migration (Vaynberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The C-terminal α-helix of PINCH1 is required for the IPP-mediated bundling of F-actin.
source: Previously, the C-terminal α-helix of PINCH1 has been shown to directly interact with actin and is required for the IPP-mediated bundling of F-actin, a process important for cell spreading and migration (Vaynberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The Rsu1 and actin binding surfaces on PINCH1_LIM5C largely overlap with each other.
source: By comparing the Rsu1 and actin binding surfaces on PINCH1_LIM5C, we found that these two binding surfaces largely overlap with each other (Figure 4A), suggesting that the binding of Rsu1 to PINCH1 interferes with the binding of actin to PINCH1.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The binding of Rsu1 to PINCH1 interferes with the binding of actin to PINCH1.
source: By comparing the Rsu1 and actin binding surfaces on PINCH1_LIM5C, we found that these two binding surfaces largely overlap with each other (Figure 4A), suggesting that the binding of Rsu1 to PINCH1 interferes with the binding of actin to PINCH1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structural overlap of binding surfaces.

claim: Wild-type Rsu1 but not the DY/KK mutant of Rsu1 forms a complex with IPP.
source: To test our hypothesis, we first purified the IPP complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and confirmed that Rsu1 binds to the IPP complex in a PINCH1-dependent way, as the wild-type Rsu1 but not the DY/KK mutant of Rsu1 forms a complex with IPP (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gel filtration data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Rsu1 binds to the IPP complex in a PINCH1-dependent way.
source: To test our hypothesis, we first purified the IPP complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and confirmed that Rsu1 binds to the IPP complex in a PINCH1-dependent way, as the wild-type Rsu1 but not the DY/KK mutant of Rsu1 forms a complex with IPP (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the PINCH1-binding deficient mutant does not bind IPP.

claim: The actin-bundling ability of IPP complex was inhibited with the presence of Rsu1 in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the actin-bundling ability of IPP complex was inhibited with the presence of Rsu1 in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by actin bundling assay data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The PINCH1-binding deficient mutants of Rsu1, Y140K, and DY/KK, were unable to interfere with the IPP-mediated F-actin bundling.
source: In contrast, the PINCH1-binding deficient mutants of Rsu1, Y140K, and DY/KK, even with a much higher concentration than wild-type Rsu1, were unable to interfere with the IPP-mediated F-actin bundling (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by actin bundling assay data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Either the length or the number of bundled actins was decreased by the addition of wild-type Rsu1, but not the Y140K or DY/KK mutants.
source: The detailed quantification further indicated that either the length or the number of bundled actins was decreased by the addition of wild-type Rsu1, but not the Y140K or DY/KK mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Rsu1 or its Y140K mutant could not bundle F-actin by itself.
source: As a control, Rsu1 or its Y140K mutant could not bundle F-actin by itself, while the DY/KK mutant of Rsu1 weakly promotes F-actin bundling (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), presumably induced by the artificial interaction between the introduced positively charged residues and actin.
evidence: This claim is supported by actin bundling assay data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The DY/KK mutant of Rsu1 weakly promotes F-actin bundling.
source: As a control, Rsu1 or its Y140K mutant could not bundle F-actin by itself, while the DY/KK mutant of Rsu1 weakly promotes F-actin bundling (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), presumably induced by the artificial interaction between the introduced positively charged residues and actin.
evidence: This claim is supported by actin bundling assay data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The electron microscopic analysis showed some large actin bundles in the F-actin sample with the IPP complex, but not in the F-actin sample with the IPP/Rsu1 mixture.
source: In addition, the electron microscopic analysis showed some large actin bundles in the F-actin sample with the IPP complex, but not in the F-actin sample with the IPP/Rsu1 mixture (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Wild-type Rsu1 localized to the FA while the PINCH1-binding deficient mutants (Y140K and DY/KK) failed to accumulate at the FA.
source: To validate the cellular effect of Rsu1 on F-actin bundling, we overexpressed different Rsu1 variants in HeLa cells, the immortal human cervical cancer cells, and found that the wild-type Rsu1 localized to the FA while the PINCH1-binding deficient mutants (Y140K and DY/KK) failed to accumulate at the FA (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Stress fibers were significantly decreased in the cells transfected with Rsu1 while those remained largely unchanged in the cells transfected with the Y140K and DY/KK mutants.
source: Consistent with the inhibitory role of Rsu1 in the IPP-mediated actin bundling, stress fibers were significantly decreased in the cells transfected with Rsu1 while those remained largely unchanged in the cells transfected with the Y140K and DY/KK mutants (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy and quantitative data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Cell spreading was inhibited by overexpressing the wild-type Rsu1.
source: In addition, cell spreading was inhibited by overexpressing the wild-type Rsu1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell spreading assay data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The overexpression of either Y140K or DY/KK in cells showed no decrease on cell spreading.

claim: Cells tightly control the Rsu1 level for the homeostasis of actin dynamics.
source: It is likely that cells tightly control the Rsu1 level for the homeostasis of actin dynamics, as either depleting Rsu1, which reduces the cellular protein level of the IPP complex and thereby impairs IPP-mediated actin bundling (Kadrmas et al., 2004; Gonzalez-Nieves et al., 2013), or elevating the Rsu1 level, which disrupts F-actin bundles, would interfere with the actin-dependent cell motility.

The nM-scale binding affinity is achieved through a large PINCH1-binding surface on the concave part of the LRR-solenoid in Rsu1 (Figure 3A), the most common protein interaction surface on the LRR proteins (Kobe and Kajava, 2001).
